title: Gathering sparks
hook: each good act lifts a spark back to its source

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vessels couldn't hold the light, and sparks fell with the shards. Your line was broken things hold light. What cracked thing did you look at twice? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

In the book of Ruth, a widow walks into a barley field after the reapers have gone through. She isn't harvesting. She's gleaning: bending down, again and again, for the stalks that fell and were left behind. Slow work, done close to the ground, one stalk at a time. By evening she has enough to carry home to Naomi. Luria's followers gave every person a job that looks a lot like hers. The light fell. Now someone has to bend down and pick it up. Today's words.
screen: `RUTH IN THE BARLEY FIELD.` → `BENDING FOR WHAT FELL.` → `SOMEONE HAS TO PICK IT UP.`

segments.voice: Gathering sparks. In Hebrew, the lifting of the sparks. Turn it four ways. First, where the sparks are. After the breaking, Luria's teaching says, sparks of holy light lie scattered, wrapped in husks. The Hebrew word is kelipot: shells or peels that hide the light the way a peel hides the fruit. Second, who gathers. In this picture, people do. A commandment kept, an act of kindness, a blessing said with care: each one frees a spark from its husk and lifts it back toward its source. For Luria's followers, the commandments weren't only rules. They were a way of gathering. Third, the ordinary places. Hasidic teachers carried this out into daily life and found sparks everywhere: in the food on a plate, in the tools of a trade, on the road to work. Eat with a blessing, deal honestly, speak kindly, and the thing in your hand is lifted. Some Hasidic stories say a person is led to a certain town, a certain meal, a certain stranger, because a spark there was waiting for them in particular. Fourth, the size of the job. Nobody gathers all of it. Each person has their own sparks, the teaching goes, and the work happens one at a time, like Ruth bending in the field. No grand gesture. A shard, picked up and set right. That's why today's line is so small. Not the whole world yet. One shard.
screen: `SPARKS WRAPPED IN HUSKS.` · `GOOD ACTS LIFT THEM.` · `SPARKS IN ORDINARY THINGS.` · `ONE SPARK AT A TIME.` · then, large: `REPAIR A SHARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one small repair. Settle, and let your breath slow. Look around you, or through your day, for one small thing that's out of place. A loose button. A drawer that sticks. A message you never answered. A word you said too sharply yesterday. Choose just one. Picture yourself fixing it, slowly and with care, as if something hidden in it were being lifted. Notice how small it is, and let that be enough. When the bell rings, if you can, go and do it. The bell holds the time.
Gathering sparks. In Luria's teaching and in Hasidic life, each good act frees a spark from its husk and lifts it back toward its source. Today's words.
Your line: repair a shard. Today, mend one small broken thing, a button, a drawer, a message, and do it with care, as if something were being lifted. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: In Hasidic communities, the idea of lifting sparks is taught as a reason to say blessings over food and to treat work, travel and ordinary objects with care, since each can hold something holy.

myth: in this teaching, sparks are found only in holy places
Hasidic teachers found them in food, in a trade, on the road to work.
the husks are pictured like peels that hide the light
kelipot: shells around the fruit, hiding what's inside.
one person is meant to gather all the sparks
each person has their own; the work happens one at a time.

fork.setup: you sit down to an ordinary meal. in Hasidic teaching on the sparks, what can this moment be?
options: nothing much: holiness happens somewhere else.
a chance to lift a spark, by eating with a blessing.
fork.reveal: Hasidic teachers saw sparks in food itself: a blessing and a careful meal lift the spark hidden in it.

trapdoor: what you thought: sparks are just a pretty image.
what it means: holy light lies hidden in husks, and each good act frees a piece of it and lifts it home.
what a scholar hears: the Lurianic lifting of the sparks from the kelipot, carried by Hasidic teachers into eating, work, and travel.

sources.ref: Lurianic teaching on the sparks and the kelipot (Chaim Vital)
Hasidic teaching on lifting sparks (ha'alat nitzotzot), e.g. Keter Shem Tov

notes: Editor pass: cut 'young' (Ruth 2 does not give her age) and replaced 'enough to feed two people' with 'enough to carry home to Naomi', which Ruth 2:17–18 says directly.

Ruth 2 paraphrased: Ruth gleans after the reapers; 'by evening she has enough to feed two people' is a reading of 2:17–18 (she beats out an ephah and brings it to Naomi). Please confirm the phrasing; the ephah measure is left unstated.
